questions.scenario: It's the annual School Science Exhibition. What is your main contribution to the group project?

options.text: Connecting the wires, cutting the PVC pipes, and building the actual working hydraulic bridge or volcano model.
Writing down the complex formulas and making sure the underlying physics principles of the project are 100% accurate.
Designing a stunning, colorful thermocol chart and practicing how to present the project perfectly to the judges.
Managing the Rs. 500 budget given by the school, assigning tasks to friends, and organizing the materials.

questions.scenario: During the Chemistry Lab practical, you are doing the classic acid-base titration. What are you doing?

options.text: Carefully adjusting the burette tap drop-by-drop so the liquid turns exactly that perfect, light pink color.
Calculating the exact molarity and balancing the chemical equations quickly in your rough notebook.
Fascinated by the sudden color change, you think about how to film this beautifully in slow motion.
Complaining to the lab assistant about the broken pipettes and suggesting they order better quality glassware.

questions.scenario: There's a long summer power cut at night (light chali gayi), so you go to the terrace to look at the stars.

options.text: You grab your dad's old binoculars to try and spot the actual craters on the Moon or the redness of Mars.
You try to mentally identify the constellations and recall the distance of the Pole Star in light-years.
You tell your younger sibling fascinating stories about how stars are born and die, acting out a supernova.
You plan how to convince the society secretary to turn off the streetlights next week so you can host a stargazing event.

questions.scenario: You are watching an Indian educational YouTube channel explaining a new scientific discovery.

options.text: You immediately want to pause the video and try to replicate the DIY battery or magnet experiment at home.
You listen closely to the data and wonder if the mathematical reasoning they provided has any logical flaws.
You admire the awesome 3D animations, the background music, and how simply they explained a hard topic.
You analyze how many millions of views the video got and how the creator successfully monetized education.

questions.scenario: You are reading 'Wings of Fire' or learning about Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam. What impresses you the most?

options.text: How he spent hours in the lab getting his hands dirty, physically building and testing rocket parts.
The insane amount of aerodynamic calculations and physics required to make a missile fly perfectly.
How beautifully he spoke and wrote, inspiring millions of ordinary Indian students to dream big.
How he managed massive teams at ISRO and DRDO and convinced the government to fund his space projects.

questions.scenario: A weird, bright green insect is found on the curry leaf (kadi patta) plant in your balcony.

options.text: You carefully trap it in an empty jam jar, put some leaves inside, and observe how it eats and moves.
You search online to match its physical traits and find out its exact biological species name and family tree.
You take a stunning macro-photo of it with your phone and post it on your WhatsApp status with a cool 'Did you know?' fact.
You check if there are more of them destroying the plants and tell your mom to buy organic neem spray.

questions.scenario: Your mom is trying to make curd (dahi) at home during winter, but it refuses to set properly.

options.text: You suggest an experiment: wrap one bowl in a warm sweater and leave another outside to see which sets better.
You read up on the exact optimal temperature and pH level needed for Lactobacillus bacteria to multiply.
You imagine how cool an animation of the milk proteins tangling up into curd would look.
You calculate whether wasting time on homemade curd in winter is worth it compared to just buying a Rs. 20 Amul packet.

questions.scenario: Your school takes you on a picnic to the local Science City or Planetarium.

options.text: You run straight to the interactive 'Fun Science' area to pull levers, spin wheels, and touch the static electricity ball.
You stand in front of the ISRO satellite models and read every single detailed information board.
You are mesmerized by the 3D dome show of the solar system and love the narrator's deep, dramatic voice.
You notice the museum is a bit dusty and think of strategies to market it better to tourists to increase ticket sales.

questions.scenario: You buy a cheap glass prism or a set of magnets from the local stationery shop. What do you do?

options.text: You take the prism to the sunlight and physically try to burn a hole in an old newspaper.
You take out your geometry box to measure the exact angle of light refraction on a piece of white paper.
You project a beautiful rainbow onto your bedroom wall and take aesthetic photos of the spectrum.
You take them to school, show the cool tricks to your friends, and trade them for their fancy gel pens.

questions.scenario: It's the night before your 10th standard Science Board Exam. How are you revising?

options.text: You are actually holding a mirror and a spoon to recall the concave/convex reflection rules practically.
You are solving the hardest, 5-mark numerical problems from the Electricity chapter step-by-step.
You are drawing neat, color-coded diagrams of the human heart and plant cell because visuals help you remember.
You made a strict timetable, predicted which questions will definitely come, and are leading a conference call to teach your friends.

Experimental_Scientist.title: The Hands-On Discoverer (Experimental Scientist)
Experimental_Scientist.primary_match_text: You learn by doing! You are practical, curious, and love getting your hands dirty. You don't just want to read about how the universe works in a textbook; you want to test it yourself in the lab.
Experimental_Scientist.day_in_the_life: Wearing a white coat and safety goggles, mixing volatile chemicals, operating massive laser machines, and running hundreds of trials to prove a brand new theory.
Experimental_Scientist.alternative_match_text: Your practical skills would also make you a fantastic Chemical Engineer, Forensic Scientist, or Robotics Expert.
Experimental_Scientist.educational_roadmap: 11th/12th: Science (PCM/PCB). Entrance: Crack JEE, NEET, or the IAT (IISER Aptitude Test). Degree: B.Sc or BS-MS Dual Degree at premier institutes like IISER or NISER. Next Steps: Ph.D. in your specific field.

Theoretical_Scientist.title: The Deep Thinker (Theoretical Scientist)
Theoretical_Scientist.primary_match_text: You are an intellectual powerhouse. You have a highly analytical brain, love complex mathematics, and prefer using logic and data to unlock the secrets of the universe from your desk.
Theoretical_Scientist.day_in_the_life: Staring at blackboards full of complex math equations, writing deep research papers, writing computer code to simulate galaxies, and solving mysteries like dark matter.
Theoretical_Scientist.alternative_match_text: Your love for deep logic and math makes you a perfect fit for Data Science, Quantitative Finance, or Pure Mathematics.
Theoretical_Scientist.educational_roadmap: 11th/12th: Science (PCM is highly recommended). Entrance: Crack JEE Advanced, IAT, or NEST. Degree: B.Sc in Physics or Mathematics at institutes like IISc Bangalore or TIFR. Next Steps: Masters and a Ph.D.

Science_Communicator.title: The Science Storyteller (Science Communicator / Museum Curator)
Science_Communicator.primary_match_text: You sit at the beautiful intersection of Science and Art. You understand complex scientific concepts, but your true talent is breaking them down and explaining them to ordinary people in a fun, visual way.
Science_Communicator.day_in_the_life: Scripting engaging YouTube videos about black holes, designing interactive planetarium shows, writing articles for magazines like National Geographic, or designing cool museum exhibits.
Science_Communicator.alternative_match_text: Your creativity and communication skills would make you a brilliant Documentary Filmmaker, Teacher, or UX/UI Designer.
Science_Communicator.educational_roadmap: 11th/12th: Science (PCM/PCB). Degree: B.Sc in any field. Next Steps: Pursue a Master's or PG Diploma in Journalism, Mass Communication, or Science Communication.

Lab_Director.title: The Research Boss (Chief Scientist / Lab Director)
Lab_Director.primary_match_text: You are a natural leader with a sharp strategic mind. You love science, but you are more interested in the big picture—managing the money, leading the teams, and turning ideas into real-world innovations.
Lab_Director.day_in_the_life: Pitching to the government for multi-crore research grants, buying expensive lab equipment, managing a team of 50 brilliant scientists, and deciding which research projects to focus on.
Lab_Director.alternative_match_text: Your leadership skills would make you an excellent Tech Entrepreneur, R&D Manager at a massive corporation, or Management Consultant.
Lab_Director.educational_roadmap: 11th/12th: Science (PCM/PCB). Degree: B.Tech or B.Sc. Next Steps: Gain a few years of research experience, then pursue an MBA in Technology Management or a Ph.D. with a focus on administrative roles.
